source.title: Adversarial Deep Embedded Clustering: On a Better Trade-off Between Feature Randomness and Feature Drift
source.authors: Nairouz Mrabah; Mohamed Bouguessa; Riadh Ksantini

record.tranche_reason: The study cites prior work on fitting random labels as motivation, then develops ADEC to address feature randomness in clustering. Its own results concern gradient alignment in pseudo-label clustering, not fitting randomly labeled images.
record.gate_note: The paper states that Zhang et al. showed networks fit random labels, but that is cited prior work, not a result of this study. The study's own ΔFR results measure gradient alignment for pseudo-labels; they do not test random-label fitting, training time, unstructured inputs, label-noise degradation, regularization effects on random-label fitting, or learning order.
record.test_reason: Section 3.1 uses Zhang et al.'s random-label fitting result to motivate feature randomness in clustering. The study's own experiments compare clustering performance and gradient alignment; none measure fitting random labels or another claim version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that ADEC improves the trade-off between feature randomness and feature drift, supported by gradient comparisons and clustering experiments. They also report improved clustering ACC and NMI against their baselines.
record.recipe_differences: ADEC uses adversarial regularization and clustering experiments; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports IDEC* learning curves are sensitive to γ: only γ = 0.01 yields an acceptable curve. This concerns clustering performance, not the claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: During MNIST clustering, ADEC has higher average alignment with the true supervised gradient than IDEC*, according to Section 5.3.2 and Figure 7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this clustering setup, adversarial regularization produces better gradient alignment with true supervision than vanilla reconstruction regularization.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
record.problems: The ΔFR comparison is presented in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The reported gradient-alignment measure is not a direct measure of random-label fitting.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows: the cited random-label result is prior work, and the other reported clustering metrics do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Training and test error under completely random labels with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative time to fit true versus random labels and convergence across label-corruption fractions.
Zero-error fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and steady test-error degradation across random-label corruption fractions.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether their removal harms true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-data patterns before memorizing noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: Pseudo-label gradient alignment does not establish random-label memorization or the order in which signal and noise are learned. The execution-time comparisons concern different clustering methods, not true-label versus random-label fitting.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label training error, test error, architecture and hyperparameter invariance.
Training time and convergence as label corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test error across corruption fractions.
Effects of weight decay, dropout or augmentation on fitting random labels and true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: ADEC
rows.operation_detail: Measured ΔFR, defined as cosine similarity between the pseudo-supervised and true supervised loss gradients, during MNIST training.
rows.value: Figure 7; the text says ADEC's average ΔFR values are considerably higher than IDEC*'s.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison but no plotted values. This gradient-alignment measure does not show random-label training error.
rows.check: ADEC's gradient alignment relative to IDEC* is the study's method-performance comparison, not a measure of any claim version. The qualitative direction is stated in Section 5.3.2, although numerical values are unavailable in the supplied text.

rows.subject: IDEC*
rows.operation_detail: Measured ΔFR, defined as cosine similarity between the pseudo-supervised and true supervised loss gradients, during MNIST training.
rows.value: Figure 7; the text says ADEC's average ΔFR values are considerably higher than IDEC*'s.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison but no plotted values. IDEC* is the model obtained by replacing ADEC's adversarial mechanism with vanilla reconstruction.
rows.check: IDEC* is the comparator in the same gradient-alignment experiment. This row does not measure random-label fitting and should remain outside the claim-evidence rows.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
